25.0.0.en: These are also proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out: [1]

25.0.1.en: These proverbs were collected under the guidance of the Holy Spirit of God. Three centuries after the death of Solomon, some scribes "copied them out," that is, transcribed and transmitted them in writing. They were called the men of Hezekiah, and the Septuagint calls them "the friends of Hezekiah."

25.0.2.en: Hezekiah was a good king, a man of peace and reform; in his reign there was progress in the fields of art and literature, and the leaders and the people took interest in religious life. For where there is a good leader, the people enjoy a holy character and care for their salvation.

25.0.3.en: We learn from 2 Chr 29:25-30; 31:21 that Hezekiah took care to restore the order that the prophet David had set for the service of the temple, and God rewarded him for his concern for the movement of religious reform by the discovery of this collection of proverbs after it had remained hidden for three centuries. This was like the discovery by the men of the good Josiah of a copy of the Law (2 Chr 34:14-16).

25.0.4.en: Some see that this addition was made under the guidance of such men as Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah.

25.1.0.en: 2 It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter. 3 The heaven for height, and the earth for depth, and the heart of kings is unsearchable. 4 Take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer. 5 Take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness. 6 Put not forth thyself in the presence of the king, and stand not in the place of great men: 7 For better it is that it be said unto thee, Come up hither; than that thou shouldest be put lower in the presence of the prince whom thine eyes have seen.

25.1.1.en: It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter [2].

25.1.2.en: It befits the king to realize that the things of God, His wisdom and His plan, cannot be penetrated to their depths as they are. As the Apostle Paul says: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?" (Rom 11:33-34; Deut 29:29). The things of God cannot be searched out, for He alone knows the secrets of Himself, but the king is obliged to search out every matter to which he puts his hand or which he seriously considers, so that his decision may be sound. For the glory of the king is not in his authority and his commands, but in searching out matters in the spirit of wisdom.

25.1.3.en: When the king realizes that the things of God cannot be searched out, he is filled with the fear of the Lord, and takes into account that there is One higher than the high, who is above all, so he is obliged in all his conduct to fear God and revere Him.

25.1.4.en: Since God has made the believing man a king with authority, he is obliged to search out the matter, that is, to practice everything after a deep study of the word of God and knowledge of the will of God, so that he may become an object of His pleasure. The Lord Christ says: "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me" (Jn 5:39). And the Apostle says: "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth" (2 Tim 2:15).

25.1.5.en: * Consider what is said in the Psalms: "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it" (Ps 139:6). And Solomon says: "It is the glory of God to conceal a thing" (Prov 25:2). For this reason I have often decided to stop and not write. Believe me, this is what I did. But lest I cause you disappointment, and lest my silence lead those who asked me into ungodliness, and they give themselves up to dispute, I pressed myself to write briefly what I now send to your holiness.

25.1.6.en: Pope Athanasius the Apostolic: * Even if all minds gathered together to search together, and tongues cooperated to speak together, as I have said, no one will be able to reach a satisfactory conclusion in this matter.

25.2.0.en: St. Basil the Great: The heaven for height, and the earth for depth, and the heart of kings is unsearchable [3].

25.2.1.en: With the height of the heavens, man has been granted to examine the stars through the science of astronomy, and with the depth of the earth he has been granted to examine the treasures in its interior, such as minerals, petroleum, and so on; but the heart of the true believer united with God cannot be searched out; for the Lord Christ Himself says: "the kingdom of God is within you" (Lk 17:21). And the Apostle says: "ye are the temple of the living God; as God hath said, I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people" (2 Cor 6:16). Who then can search out the kingdom of God, and know the details of His temple in which the Holy Spirit dwells?

25.3.0.en: Take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer [4].

25.4.0.en: Take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness [5].

25.4.1.en: The purifying of silver from dross allows the silversmith to form a precious silver vessel, and the removal of evil from the heart makes of it a temple for the Spirit of God, the Giver of sanctification. And the removal of wicked counsellors from before the king establishes his throne in righteousness. This is what Solomon did, as he condemned the doers of evil around him before beginning his kingly work (1 Kgs 2).

25.4.2.en: This is also what will happen on the great day of the Lord, when the King of kings comes and crushes the devil and his kingdom, and casts him with his hosts and followers into the lake burning with fire, to declare His eternal heavenly kingdom, and be glorified in His elect forever.

25.4.3.en: In the same spirit it befits the Church to cast out the wicked one, and remove the corrupt leaven, lest it leaven the whole lump.

25.4.4.en: This is also what the believer experiences in his daily life, where the roots of evil must be plucked out while good is planted by the work of divine grace. As the psalmist says: "Depart from evil, and do good; and dwell for evermore" (Ps 37:27).

25.4.5.en: * Why is it said: "Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the LORD" (Ps 118:1)? Scripture here specifies "who walk," not "who have walked," those who walk in the doing of good and find their delight in doing it... As for those who flee from evil... they cannot be praised if they manage to avoid sin once or twice, unless they are able to cut it off from their lives completely... If we want what is good, let us begin by avoiding evils... "Depart from evil, and do good" (Ps 37:27): the Psalm sketches for us the way of virtue... with knowledge and skill... For departing from evil is the beginning of good... If perfect virtue were demanded from the beginning, you would draw back before you began.

25.5.0.en: St. Basil the Great: Put not forth thyself in the presence of the king, and stand not in the place of great men [6].

25.6.0.en: For better it is that it be said unto thee, Come up hither; than that thou shouldest be put lower in the presence of the prince whom thine eyes have seen [7].

25.6.1.en: It befits the believer not to push himself to appear before rulers, nor to desire to sit with them in order to obtain the honor of men.

25.6.2.en: When the palaces of emperors and great men were opened to the men of the Church by the conversion of Constantine to the Christian faith, there was another race to flee to the wilderness to enjoy sitting with God in the stillness of the wilderness, as St. Abba Anthony the Great did.

25.6.3.en: The Lord Christ says: "When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room; lest a more honourable man than thou be bidden of him; and he that bade thee and him come and say to thee, Give this man place; and thou begin with shame to take the lowest room. But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have glory in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee. For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted" (Lk 14:7-11).

25.6.4.en: The pride that drives man to present himself in the presence of the great shatters man's life before himself as before others, and deserves God's rebuke. But whoever is humbled in his depths with sincerity and devotion, God exalts. As St. Mary said: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree" (Lk 1:52).

25.6.5.en: If he who pushes himself to obtain vain honors and glories from the world deserves blame, what of the believer who pushes himself in spiritual and religious fields seeking temporal glory?

25.6.6.en: * Let the proud seek earthly kingdoms and love them, but "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

25.6.7.en: * The Lord sat in the house of a proud Pharisee (Lk 7:36), as I said, He was in his house but not in his heart, but He did not enter the house of the centurion, and yet He possessed his heart (Mt 8:8).

25.6.8.en: Zacchaeus also received the Lord in his house and in his heart (Lk 19:6). As for the centurion's faith, it was praised because of his humility, for he said: "I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof." The Lord said: "Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel" (Mt 8:10), this according to the flesh, for according to the Spirit he is an "Israelite." Christ came to the Israelites according to the flesh, that is, to the Jews, seeking first the lost sheep among this people, taking His body also from this people. He said: "I have not found so great faith." We can measure the faith of men as men judge it, but the Lord, who sees what is within, and whom no one deceives, bore witness to the heart of this man as he listened to words of humility and announced a word of healing.

25.6.9.en: * As soon as you become proud, you immediately lose what you have received.

25.6.10.en: St. Augustine: * Humility is granted to each person according to the degree of his greatness. Pride is harmful to everyone. It seeks to corrupt, through themselves, those who are great!

25.6.11.en: St. Jerome: * What madness! Does not this proud man know that his glory passes away and evaporates like a dream, and that greatness and authority are nothing but a deceptive mirage?

25.7.0.en: Go not forth hastily to strive, lest thou know not what to do in the end thereof, when thy neighbour hath put thee to shame [8].

25.7.1.en: The Lord Christ gives us a practical example in life concerning not hastening to enter into quarrels or battles with others. He says: "Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand? Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace" (Lk 14:31-32).

25.7.2.en: King Josiah committed this error; although he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord (2 Kgs 22:2), yet when Pharaoh Necho king of Egypt went up to fight against Assyria, King Josiah went up to fight him, although Pharaoh had not gone up to fight Josiah. He entered a battle at Megiddo which ended in his death (2 Kgs 23:29-30).

25.7.3.en: It befits the believer not to throw himself into battles which he could have avoided. For this reason our Lord asked us that when persecution comes in a city we flee to another, not out of fear of death, nor in cowardice and servility, but that we may not push ourselves into temptation.

25.7.4.en: * He leaves us peace as He departs, and He will give us His peace when He comes at the end. Peace He leaves us in this world, and His peace He will give us in the world to come. He leaves us His peace, and as we dwell in it we defeat the enemy.

25.7.5.en: He will give us His peace when there are no more enemies to fight and we reign as kings.

25.7.6.en: Peace He leaves us so that we may also love one another here, and He will give us His peace when we are beyond the possibility of strife.

25.7.7.en: Peace He leaves us so that one may not judge another in what is a secret to each, while we are on earth; He will give us His peace when He "will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God" (1 Cor 4:5). Yet in Him and from Him we receive peace, whether that which He leaves us as He goes to the Father or that which He will grant us when He brings us to the Father.

25.7.8.en: And what does He leave us when He ascends from us but His presence, which He will not withdraw from us? For He is our peace, who hath made both one (Eph 2:14). Therefore He becomes our peace, whether when we believe that it is He, or when we see Him as He is (1 Jn 3:2).

25.7.9.en: For if, while we are still in this corrupt body which weighs down the soul and we walk by faith, not by sight, He does not leave those who depart while they are absent from Him (2 Cor 5:6-7), how much more, when we attain that vision, will He fill us with Himself.

25.7.10.en: * The peace He leaves us in this world can more fittingly be called our peace than His peace. For since He is utterly without sin, there is in Him no element of strife itself. But the peace that is ours is that in the midst of which we still say: "Forgive us our debts" (Mt 6:12)... It is not the perfect peace, for we see another law in our members, warring against the law of our mind (Rom 7:22-23).

25.8.0.en: Debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself; and discover not a secret to another [9].

25.9.0.en: Lest he that heareth it put thee to shame, and thine infamy turn not away [10].

25.9.1.en: Not only is it unfitting for us to hasten to enter a quarrel with our neighbor, but we must also, before resorting to the courts or to the entry of a third party for reconciliation, meet with him in secret, and speak with him in a spirit of brotherhood, so that he feels that we seek reconciliation in a spirit of love, and not by justifying ourselves and exposing him.

25.9.2.en: The entry of a third party or resort to the courts may oblige him to reveal matters we did not know, and so we become a scandal. The Lord Christ commands us: "Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother. But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established..." (Mt 18:15 etc.).

25.9.3.en: * Solomon often refers to a "friend" and "friendship." So it is fitting for us now to look at what he means by friendship. He says that grace and friendship set free. Also the Savior says in the Gospels to the Jews who believed on Him: "If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed; and ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free" (Jn 8:31-32). Again Paul says: "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law" (Gal 3:13); so if friendship sets free, then Christ is the truth and the friendship. For this reason all who acquire the knowledge of Christ are friends to one another. For this the Savior calls His disciples friends (Jn 15:15), John the Baptist is the friend of the bridegroom (Jn 3:29), and so is Moses (Ex 33:11), and all the saints. And by virtue of that friendship alone the friends are friends of one another.

25.10.0.en: 11 A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver. 12 As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover upon an obedient ear. 13 As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to them that send him: for he refresheth the soul of his masters. 14 Whoso boasteth himself of a false gift is like clouds and wind without rain.

25.10.1.en: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver [11].

25.10.2.en: Some see that the discussion here is of apples beautiful in form, golden in color, set in a dish of silver. It is a wonderful sight! So is the wise word spoken at its proper time.

25.10.3.en: Ruth spoke with Boaz in words full of grace and at the proper time, and there was fulfilled for her what she had not dreamed of, that the Lord Christ should come from her seed.

25.10.4.en: And Abigail spoke wise words with David at the time of his fury, and he praised her and listened to her (1 Sam 25:32).

25.10.5.en: It is not enough that we speak the truth, but we must realize how to present it, and when to speak it and to whom.

25.10.6.en: How much we need wisdom to be our nature in our inner being, joined to our conduct and words outwardly, that is, that we bear the holiness of the inner man and also the holiness of the body with its senses, feelings, gifts, and all its energies and conduct. This wisdom (or knowledge or understanding) is a divine gift.

25.10.7.en: * The Holy Spirit, in whom are all kinds of gifts, gives to some the word of wisdom.

25.10.8.en: * Through the guidance of the Spirit man comes to the knowledge of the nature of all things.

25.10.9.en: * Send out thy light (Ps 3:43); this light sent from the Father to the mind of those called to salvation is understanding through the Spirit, who leads them to be enlightened by God.

25.10.10.en: Origen: * There is no knowledge without faith, nor faith without knowledge. The Son is the true Teacher.

25.11.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria: As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover upon an obedient ear [12].

25.11.1.en: If the rebuke comes from a wise man who bears a spirit of love and tenderness, this rebuke is counted as an ornament and an earring of gold on the ear, that is, his rebuke is counted a precious and beautiful gift.

25.11.2.en: The Second Book of Chronicles gives us a wonderful example in the rebuke of the prophet Oded to the army coming from Samaria, where he told them that the wrath had reached heaven because they had taken captive their brothers of Judah. And indeed they returned the captives after honoring them, and provided them with their needs (2 Chr 28:9-15).

25.12.0.en: As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to them that send him: for he refresheth the soul of his masters [13].

25.12.1.en: It was the custom of reapers in the Middle East to put snow in their drinks during the summer harvest to refresh them, so that they could do their work in the midst of intense heat. So the trusted messenger refreshes the souls of those who sent him, since they have no doubt of his faithfulness.

25.12.2.en: Faithfulness is an essential element in dealings within any society; the faithful husband, and also the wife, the superior and the subordinates, these and others, when they are faithful in providing the information required of them, refresh society, like snow that refreshes one suffering from intense heat.

25.12.3.en: And on the great day of the Lord we hear the divine voice: "Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord" (Mt 25:21).

25.12.4.en: * The steward who mismanages the affairs of his master and loses his possessions fears to face him; on the contrary, the steward who always manages his master's affairs well meets him with joy.

25.12.5.en: St. Jerome: * When your turn comes in the service, add to your bodily work a word of counsel and loving consolation for those you serve, so that your service, seasoned with salt (Col 4:6), may be acceptable.

25.12.6.en: Do not allow another to practice what is rightly entrusted to you, lest the reward be taken from you and given to another, so that he is enriched by your wealth while you are put to shame.

25.12.7.en: Carry out the obligations of your service with gentleness and care, as one who serves Christ. For the prophet says: "Cursed be he that doeth the work of the LORD negligently" (Jer 48:10).

25.13.0.en: Fear, as though the eyes of the Lord were upon you, for deviation comes from negligence and disregard, even if the work being done seems lowly to you. The work of service is a great work, which leads to the Kingdom. St. Basil the Great: Whoso boasteth himself of a false gift is like clouds and wind without rain [14].

25.13.1.en: When a place suffers drought and then a cloud appears, everyone eagerly awaits that it will pour down rain instead of the suffering of drought, and if the cloud is scattered without dropping rain, the people fall into a state of frustration and disappointment. Such is the state of him who boasts, asserting that he gives a gift, and does not fulfill what he promised.

25.13.2.en: When the Apostle Jude wrote about the teachers who promise their hearers to present the truth of the Gospel but are unable to carry out what they promise, he quoted what is in this verse, and wrote of them that they are "clouds they are without water, carried about of winds; trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots" (Jude 12).

25.14.0.en: By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone [15].

25.14.1.en: Two important things are required in dealing with others, namely long-suffering or slowness to anger, and the gentle, kind word. By long-suffering we quench the outburst of others' anger without our being kindled with anger, and thus we can, at the proper time, converse calmly and give others the opportunity to review themselves.

25.14.2.en: And by the kind word we break the anger of another. Perhaps among the most beautiful things in the Old Testament is David's attitude toward King Saul. Saul went down to the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel to seek David and kill him (1 Sam 26:2). And when David found Saul with his army commander and the people lying around him, Abishai asked to strike Saul and kill him at one stroke, but David refused; rather he took the spear that was at his head and the cruse of water and crossed over to the top of the mountain at a distance, and rebuked Abner for not guarding the king. Saul knew David's voice and said: "Is this thy voice, my son David?" (1 Sam 26:17). David said to him: "for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea." And Saul, after he had reflected, said: "I have sinned: return, my son David: for I will no more do thee harm... behold, I have played the fool, and have erred exceedingly..."

25.14.3.en: * There is nothing that surpasses love, and consequently there is nothing lower than anger. We must not concern ourselves with anything, however useful and necessary it may seem, in order to avoid the anger that causes disturbance, and we must not be troubled by matters, even those we consider not essential, in order to preserve the calm of love and peace without lack, for we must realize that nothing is as destructive as anger and vexation, and nothing as profitable as love.

25.14.4.en: Father Joseph: * A brother asked an elder: I want to be martyred for God. He answered him: "Whoever bears with his brother in the time of distress, he has become as one inside the furnace of the three youths."

25.14.5.en: The Garden of the Monks: * If a person becomes angry as a man, he puts an end to the anger as a Christian.

25.14.6.en: * The word that comes out of the mouth goes out like a stone thrown by the hand; it is far from being recalled or controlled... Therefore one must reflect on what will be said before the speech goes out. For after it has gone out, reflection on it is in vain.

25.15.1.en: eat so much as is sufficient for thee, lest thou be filled therewith, and vomit it [16].

25.15.2.en: Eating food in moderation is beneficial for health and spiritually, while excess in eating is harmful. So it is with all the needs of the body: excess in them is destructive to the body as well as to the soul. There is no sin in food as long as it is taken with thanksgiving and moderation.

25.15.3.en: Lack of control of the belly turns the sweetness of honey into nausea of the stomach. And lack of control of the tongue turns your wise words away from achieving their purpose.

25.15.4.en: * Yet I do not mean that we should not think of God at all times, and there is no need for my opponents to attack me with this argument, since they are always ready to attack, for we ought to remember God more often than we breathe, indeed I may say that we ought not to do anything else but that, and I am of those who hold the principle which commands us to "meditate day and night" (Ps 1:2), to declare the Lord "evening, and morning, and at noon" (Ps 55:17), to "bless the LORD at all times" (Ps 34:1), or as Moses said, "when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up" (Deut 6:7), or when we do anything else, and by this remembrance of God we become pure, and so I am not against the continual remembrance of God, but against the continual discussion of theology, and I do not oppose theology, as though it were something against godliness, but I oppose discussing it at an unsuitable time, and I am not against teaching theology, except when it exceeds the limit, for fullness and surfeit, even of honey with all its sweetness, cause vomiting (Prov 25:16), and for everything there is a time, as I see and as wise Solomon sees, and what is good is not good if the time is not suitable; flowers are quite out of season in winter, and men's clothes do not suit women, nor women's clothes men. Excessive laughter is not fitting during mourning, nor weeping at a drinking party. If all these are unsuitable because they are at an unsuitable time, shall we neglect choosing the suitable time only in discussing theology, though observing the suitable time for this discussion is of the utmost importance?

25.15.5.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus: * As moderation and abstaining from extravagance are usually the children of contentment, if a man is accustomed to it he does without everything that is superfluous and unnecessary, so that there may be no deviation or falling into temptations, being content with what is necessary and needful for health and for the blessed life according to the teaching of the heavenly Word, to whom be glory. Let the clothing of women be simple, neat, and well-formed, and there is no harm in using fine fabrics, those that are not suitable for men, but without wounding their modesty, and leading them to extravagance. And clothing must suit age, person, build, nature, and conduct, for the divine Apostle counsels us by saying: "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof" (Rom 13:14).

25.16.0.en: Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour's house; lest he be weary of thee, and so hate thee [17].

25.16.1.en: Again he speaks of moderation in everything, even in our relations with our relatives. With our great love for them, we must set limits in our conduct, so that we do not poke our nose into their lives, nor ask them about personal matters, nor be curious about their lives and conduct; and we set limits to our visits, and the length of the visit, however welcoming they are to us.

25.16.2.en: Let us lengthen our time of meeting God in secret and speaking with Him, and let us lessen as much as we can our meeting with people and speaking with them.

25.16.3.en: * As for the apostles and prophets, act according to the teaching of the Gospel, thus:

25.16.4.en: Receive every apostle who comes to you as the Lord (Mt 10:40).

25.16.5.en: But he must not stay more than one day, and if need be he stays another day; if he stays three days he is a false prophet.

25.17.0.en: A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow [18].

25.17.1.en: False witness or slander of a person resembles a hammer with which a man strikes the minds of others, or a club that crushes what is beneath it, or a sword or an arrow that destroys. But the believer, even if he is attacked by slander, counts this as permitted by God to discipline him, prove him, and gain the one who slandered him.

25.17.2.en: When Shimei the son of Gera cursed David, and was throwing stones at him and at the servants of the king and the mighty men around him, Abishai said to the king: "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? let me go over, I pray thee, and take off his head" (2 Sam 16:9). But the king, who was fleeing from the face of Absalom his son, said: "So let him curse, because the LORD hath said unto him, Curse David. Who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so?" And David said to Abishai and to all his servants: "Behold, my son, which came forth of my bowels, seeketh my life: how much more now may this Benjamite do it? let him alone, and let him curse; for the LORD hath bidden him" (2 Sam 16:11).

25.17.3.en: * He who is struck with a stone goes to a physician, but sharper than a stone are the blows of slander (the defaming of reputation). As Solomon says: false witness is war with a club and a sword and a sharp arrow" (see Prov 25:18), and its wounds can be healed by truth alone. If truth is destroyed, the wounds become worse and worse.

25.18.0.en: Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint [19].

25.18.1.en: The man who gains an important position of work and is trusted, and is a traitor, is exposed, and is counted as broken teeth and dislocated feet. Instead of helping others he becomes a cause of troubles and unrest. The most serious example of this is Judas, who was chosen as a disciple, and was entrusted with the treasury, and behold, he betrays his Master.

25.18.2.en: * The disciples heard that their Teacher would be killed by the Jews and were pained, and heard that one of them would betray Him and were troubled.

25.18.3.en: I wonder who goes out from the choir of our Lord's light, and goes and mingles with the darkness in great terror.

25.18.4.en: I wonder who leaves the company of the sun of fair rays, and walks in the way full of clouds and darkness.

25.18.5.en: Who is this lamb who turned himself over and became a wolf, and began to bite the good Shepherd?

25.18.6.en: Policy forced Peter to deny the Son, but no one forced Judas to betray... And when Judas asked: Is it I? the Lord answered him: Thou hast said. As one who says to him: No one forced you.

25.18.7.en: If you say: Why did He who knows all choose him when He knew he was a deceiver...? He chose him when he was good and pure and there was no fault in him, for he was gentle and upright. And after He chose him, being worthy and full of goodness, he changed and destroyed his goodness and became rejected...

25.18.8.en: The Son of God promised Judas the throne, and when he denied Him, He brought him down and left him to the gallows...

25.18.9.en: Where do you leave your throne and your glory, O chosen one? Who will give you a high throne like yours...?

25.18.10.en: The sick whom You healed weep bitterly over you; the lepers whom You cleansed bow because of your fall.

25.18.11.en: Tremble, you who are set apart, at deceitful kisses, for by one deceitful kiss the Son of God was hung on a tree.

25.18.12.en: The devil who taught Judas to betray his Teacher came back and taught him to hang himself, so that by both he might inherit the Hades for which he was qualified.

25.19.0.en: As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, and as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart [20].

25.19.1.en: The consolation of the sorrowful is not accomplished by offering him one of the songs, even if he loves it, nor by asking him to sing as the Babylonians did. They asked the Israelites in the land of captivity to praise for them with one of the songs of the Lord. As the psalmist says: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof. For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion. How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?" (Ps 137:1-4).

25.19.2.en: The Apostle says: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15). And the wise man says: "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance" (Eccl 3:4).

25.19.3.en: Whoever does not consider the feelings of the sorrowful and heavy of heart, and instead of sharing his sorrow sings, is like one who takes off the clothes of a man suffering from bitter cold, thus doubling his distress, or like one who put vinegar on nitre, so that it reacts with it and foam is produced.

25.19.4.en: * I suffer and grieve with our fellow believers who fell and denied the faith during the bitterness of persecution; they draw away a part of our hearts with them, and have caused us a similar grief by their wounds.

25.19.5.en: St. Cyprian: * Our sufferings have thus reached the ends of the inhabited world; when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.

25.19.6.en: St. Basil: * General sharing in everything, in good things and in sorrowful ones, is the only way to attain the perfection of fellowship.

25.20.0.en: 21 If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: 22 For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee.

25.20.1.en: If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink [21].

25.20.2.en: The Apostle Paul quoted these two verses, except for the last clause, from the Septuagint (Rom 12:20).

25.20.3.en: The man of God offers love with the gift, and kindles a fire of love on the head of the one who troubles him, turning his anger and fury into friendship and love. The Lord Christ commanded us: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you" (Mt 5:44).

25.21.0.en: For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee [22].

25.21.1.en: When we give the hungry enemy food and the thirsty drink, we must aim at his repentance, longing that he share with us our life full of love for God and men. This repentance is kindled in his heart with inner fires according to the good pleasure of God. But some give food and drink with the aim of pride and of belittling the enemy or making a fool of him; this is not fitting for the believer.

25.21.2.en: * The Apostle Paul teaches us in perfect clarity that almsgiving is offered to everyone, for he says: "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith" (Gal 6:10). This is quite clear enough that in works of this kind priority is given to the righteous (in giving).. This does not mean that we close our hearts toward others, even toward sinners, and even toward those who hold a hostile attitude toward us. Christ Himself says, above all: "Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you" (Lk 6:27). This matter did not pass in silence in the Old Testament; you see that we read in it: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink," a text which the Apostle used in the New Testament (Rom 12:20).

25.21.3.en: * This (scriptural) statement seems to command the committing of a crime or the practicing of a vice. But it is symbolic speech guiding us to share in the sufferings of the Lord... Scripture says: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink." This, without doubt, commands tenderness, but the continuation is: "For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head"; you may think that it commands a crime of malice. Do not doubt that it is a symbolic expression. For while it can be interpreted in two ways, one inclines toward harm, and the other interpretation inclines toward good love which calls him to leave harm and cling to tenderness, so you understand the coals as the fiery laments of repentance by which a person's pride is healed and he grieves that he is an enemy to the one who soothes his distress.

25.22.0.en: The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue [23].

25.22.1.en: It befits us not to welcome or encourage the one with a slanderous tongue who gnaws at people's honor and criticizes others in their absence, but to meet him as with a frowning face. Thus he does not go on with his destructive talk.

25.22.2.en: The Book of Proverbs repeats the necessity of peace and love in the family (Prov 21:9) and among friends, because it is a grave matter, without which the family, like society, turns into an unbearable hell.

25.23.0.en: It is better to dwell in the corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman and in a wide house [24].

25.23.1.en: * We have been commanded to love our neighbor as ourselves, therefore the first obligation of man under God's economy is to love his wife and children. By this saying I wish to assure you that you know that the responsibility of the man, as of the woman also, is their household.

25.23.2.en: Since God has set up this order in mankind itself, husbands and wives and children, it is reasonable that we should fulfill the law of love in the home first. Above all, who has more opportunity to experience our love, our peace, and our long-suffering than those who live with us? Whom must we seek to love first, besides those whom we can serve and care for the more?

25.23.3.en: Yes, we may take care of everything for our families for their material comfort and possessions, but if we fail to offer them the love of God, the Apostle shows the truth of our hearts, that it is worse than unbelievers (1 Tim 5:8). He says this to awaken our understanding, that God desires heavenly peace to rule our homes, flowing from those in charge in love toward those who are called to obey in love.

25.23.4.en: In order to manage our households, those who give orders must do so in godliness, and not with hardness of heart, or with a kind of authority without understanding or tenderness...

25.23.5.en: The righteous man, that is, he who lives by faith, is like a traveler heading toward the heavenly city, and those who give directions and commands in truth serve those who appear to be commanded...

25.23.6.en: As you exercise authority, do not fall into pride because of your position, but rather exercise spiritual authority in your homes. You are ruled by the love of God, which encourages, hopes, believes, and will never fail (1 Cor 13).

25.23.7.en: St. Augustine: * "That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands" (Titus 2:4).

25.23.8.en: The Apostle says that the older women are to advise the young women to love their husbands, because the chief of the goods of the household is that the wife be in agreement with her husband. If this happens there is no evil at all. For how can there be no peace when the body agrees with the head...? If the head is in peace, who can remove or prevent peace...? This is more useful to the household than money, nobility of birth, and power...

25.23.9.en: By love all resistance vanishes; if the husband is a pagan he quickly accepts the faith, and if he is a Christian he becomes better.

25.23.10.en: Did you see how Paul, who works with all his effort to draw us away from worldly things, gives great attention to what concerns the state of the household? For if households are well managed, spiritual things find a place, and without a sound household spiritual things are ruined...

25.23.11.en: For when a woman is married to an unbelieving man and is not virtuous, it is impossible that God not be slandered because of her, but if she is adorned with preaching she wins honor from her preaching and her good works.

25.23.12.en: Let the women whose husbands are harsh or unbelieving hear and be disciplined, so that they may lead them to good worship. For if you do not win him or persuade him to share with you in the upright teachings, you close his mouth and do not let him blaspheme the Christian religion. And this is not a simple matter, for the religion is praised because of our conduct.

25.23.13.en: St. John Chrysostom: * He who marries knows how rarely we find a wife without these faults, therefore the great orator Varius Geminus said well: "The man who does not quarrel is a bachelor." In truth: "It is better to dwell in the corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman and in a wide house." If a house shared between husband and wife makes the wife proud, and she shows contempt toward the husband, what if the wife is the richer, and the husband a refugee in her house!

25.24.0.en: As cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country [25].

25.24.1.en: What is the good news but the coming of the Lord Christ Himself, the Word of God, who is able to satisfy the soul and water it with the waters of His love? He causes to spring forth within it a fountain of living water, and it in turn waters many by the work of His Holy Spirit in it and in them.

25.24.2.en: * Scripture says: "As cold waters to a thirsty soul," so is the knowledge of our Lord Jesus, the giver of life to the mind that loves knowledge. Therefore let us draw from the holy springs, the living, life-giving waters, the rational spiritual waters. Let us take what quenches our thirst and not stop drinking. For in these matters there is a constant need for instruction beyond imagination, and greed is highly praised.

25.25.0.en: A righteous man falling down before the wicked is as a troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring [26].

25.25.1.en: The soul of the righteous and upright man is filled with distress when he finds himself obliged to submit to a wicked, corrupt man, and he is like a traveler who sees a spring of water and runs to it to drink, and behold it is full of filth, or finds a fountain and finds it full of algae.

25.26.0.en: It is not good to eat much honey: so for men to search their own glory is not glory [27].

25.26.1.en: Excess in taking honey harms the stomach and causes nausea in a person; such is the state of the man who lives not to serve others with love and in true inner humility, but seeks his own glory.

25.26.2.en: St. John Chrysostom was moved before the long-suffering of the Lord Christ even in His dealing with the devil during the temptation, for he says: [He was neither angry nor aroused, but with extreme gentleness He argued with him a second time from Scripture... teaching us that we overcome Satan not by working miracles, but by endurance and long-suffering, so that we do nothing for the sake of boasting and vainglory.]

25.26.3.en: * Just as Christ "took upon him the form of a servant" (Phil 2:7) and overcame Satan by humility, so in the beginning man fell through pride and vainglory by the deceit of the serpent?

25.26.4.en: St. Macarius the Great: * Nothing is acceptable to God like a man's counting himself the last of all; this is the first principle of practical wisdom, for the humble man, wounded in his heart, does not love vainglory, nor is he wrathful, nor does he envy his neighbor, nor does he resort to any lust.
